name: Mbure
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source.
catalog_citation: Boyd, Virginia Lee. 2015. The phonological systems of the Mbam languages of Cameroon: a focus on vowels and vowel harmony. LOT Dissertation Series 410. Utrecht: LOT. (open PDF, lotpublications.nl/Documents/)
catalog_locator: sec. 2.9.5 Tone (Mbure phonological overview), pp. 200-202; sec. 2.9.5.1-2.9.5.2
catalog_quote: Mbure has a two-tone system underlyingly, high and low. Contour melodies are caused by glide formation from syllable mergers and by the historical reduction from disyllabic to monosyllable roots. Unlike in some of the other Mbam languages, there is no indication of a loss of contrast of tone melodies in utterance-final position in connection with vowel devoicing or elision. ... Only high and low melodies are found in short syllable CV or CVC (monomoraic) noun roots. However, in bimoraic noun roots, CṼ: (CVN), CVⁿC and CVCV noun roots, all four tone melodies are attested ... Noun prefixes usually have a low tone, although there are a few exceptions. ... All four possible underlying tone melodies have been found for Mbure verb roots: L, HL H and LH. In verb stems which contain two or more suffixes, and a H melody, the H spreads to the right to the penultimate syllable. It is assumed that …

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim in the Boyd 2015 text we hold at sec. 2.9.5-2.9.5.2, printed pp. 200-201 (locator says 200-202; trivial). The record's claim that the book never mentions stress/accent for Mbure also checks (single hit is a quoted Dixon & Aikhenvald checklist in ch. 3). (2) Deciding source: a 2015 Leiden PhD/LOT monograph by an SIL fieldworker with her own Mbure corpus; the Mbure chapter is a 21-page phonological overview. It is the only phonological description of this language in Glottolog (the other two entries are a 1982 SIL survey report and a 1992 19-page sociolinguistic survey), so it is the best available and we hold it. (3) list of works to obtain: nothing that would plausibly improve the classification; Scruggs 1982 listed at low priority for completeness only
